Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A professor invites me to his “Black Lit” class; they’re reading Larson’s Passing. One of the black students says, “Sometimes light-skinned blacks think they can fool other blacks, but I can always tell,” looking right through me. After I tell them I am black, I ask the class, “Was I passing when I was just sitting here, before I told you?” A white woman shakes her head desperately, as if I had deliberately deceived her. She keeps examining my face, then turning away as if she hopes I’ll disappear. Why presume “passing” is based on what I leave out and not what she fills in? In one scene in the book, in a restaurant, she’s “passing,” though no one checked her at the door— “Hey, you black?” My father, who looked white, told me this story: every year when he’d go to get his driver’s license, the man at the window filling out the form would ask, “White or black?” pencil poised, without looking up. My father wouldn’t pass, but he might use silence to trap a devil. When he didn’t speak, the man would look up at my father’s face. “What did he write?” my father quizzed me.

At the invitation of a professor, I sat in on his African American literature course while the students were discussing Nella Larsen’s novel *Passing*. After I disclosed my own Black heritage, I challenged the group by asking whether my quiet presence prior to my revelation constituted "passing." In response, a white female student shook her head in deep distress, acting as though I had deliberately manipulated her. She alternated between intently scrutinizing my features and looking away, as if hoping I would simply vanish. 

This reaction raised a fundamental question: why is "passing" assumed to be defined by what I choose to conceal, rather than the assumptions the observer projects onto me? This dynamic appears in Larsen’s book during a restaurant scene, where a character "passes" simply because no one at the entrance stopped to interrogate her racial identity. 

My father, whose physical appearance was white, used to share a story that reflected this idea. Every year when renewing his driver's permit, the clerk filling out the paperwork would hold his pencil ready over the form and ask, "White or black?" without ever raising his eyes. Rather than actively pretending to be white, my father used quiet hesitation as a way to expose the man's underlying biases. By withholding an answer, he compelled the clerk to finally look up and examine his face. Afterward, my father would test me by asking, "Which box do you think he marked?"

***

During a literature seminar centered on the trope of racial passing, a striking disconnect emerged between academic analysis and reality. As the students analyzed stories of individuals navigating the color line, they failed to recognize the Black identity of their own narrator, relying entirely on visual cues and superficial appearances. When the narrator finally disclosed their race, the revelation disrupted the classroom's dynamics. A white classmate reacted with immediate defensiveness, acting as though she had been intentionally deceived. This reaction laid bare a fundamental human truth: people rely so heavily on their initial visual assumptions that when those assumptions are proven wrong, they often blame the individual for "tricking" them rather than questioning their own biases.

This classroom encounter prompted the narrator to reexamine and challenge the conventional definition of "passing." Traditionally, passing is viewed as a deliberate, deceptive act—a conscious effort by an individual to conceal their heritage and blend into a privileged group. However, the narrator argues that passing is less about active deception and more about audience projection. It is not necessarily something a person *does*, but rather something that is *done to them* by an observer who projects their own rigid expectations of race onto another person's body. In this sense, "passing" occurs in the mind of the beholder.

To illustrate how this passive categorization functions in everyday life, the narrator recalls an experience involving their father at a driver’s license bureau. While processing the paperwork, a clerk casually checked a box assigning a racial category to the father based solely on a quick glance. The clerk never asked for confirmation, and the father never offered a correction; the system simply recorded what the clerk assumed to be true. 

Through these combined experiences—in the classroom and at the bureaucratic counter—the text demonstrates that racial categorization often operates through passive, unexamined judgments. Ultimately, the burden of "passing" rests not on the individual being perceived, but on a society that mistakes its own visual assumptions for objective truth.

**Title:** The Eye of the Beholder: Projection, Perception, and the Illusion of "Passing"

We like to believe that our eyes are objective recorders of the world, capturing reality in crisp, unadulterated detail. When it comes to race, modern society often treats visual cues—skin tone, hair texture, bone structure—as an undeniable, biological index of identity. Yet, race is rarely something we merely see; it is something we read, interpreted through a complex web of cultural conditioning, social expectations, and personal biases. The phenomenon of "passing"—traditionally understood as a light-skinned person of color deliberately posing as white—exposes the profound instability of this visual system. By examining both literary representations and lived experiences, it becomes clear that racial identity is not simply projected by the individual, but actively constructed by the mind of the observer.

This dynamic frequently unfolds in the academic classroom during discussions of Nella Larsen’s 1929 Harlem Renaissance novel, *Passing*. In teaching or analyzing the text, one quickly notices how deeply students rely on a binary framework to make sense of the characters, Irene Redfield and Clare Kendry. Inevitably, a student will express bewilderment regarding how Clare manages to pass as a white woman in high-society Chicago, even marrying an avowedly racist white man who remains entirely oblivious to her lineage. "How could he not *know*?" students often ask, searching the text for somatic clues or evidence of elaborate deception. 

Yet, as classroom debate deepens, the answer becomes obvious: Clare’s husband, John Bellew, does not fail to see her Blackness because she is an extraordinary actress, but because his own racial worldview does not permit him to see it. To Bellew, a wealthy, beautiful woman in an exclusive hotel *must* be white. His brain automatically fills in the blanks, smoothing over any physical ambiguities to align with his social assumptions. In the classroom, as students debate where the "deception" lies, they begin to realize that the act of passing in Larsen's novel is less about a cunning disguise and more about the blind spots of the white gaze.

This literary insight mirrors the quiet, everyday realities of my own family history. Growing up, I listened to stories about my maternal grandmother, a woman whose light complexion, hazel eyes, and soft waves of hair routinely threw strangers into a state of cognitive dissonance. My grandmother never denied her Black heritage, nor did she ever attempt to actively deceive anyone; she simply walked through the world as herself. Yet, her racial identity shifted depending entirely on who was looking at her and where she happened to be standing.

When she entered an upscale downtown department store in the 1950s, white shopkeepers greeted her with deference, assuming she was one of their own. If she walked down the street holding the hand of her darker-skinned sister, passersby would cast bewildered looks, scrambling to make sense of the visual mismatch—often concluding my grandmother was a white employer, a light-skinned Latin American visitor, or a benevolent benefactor. She was not tricking anyone. Rather, people were constantly projecting their own rigid racial categories onto her canvas. They saw what their subconscious biases dictated they *should* see based on context, class, and companion. 

These twin vantage points—the literary space of Larsen’s novel and the personal realm of family memory—converge on a singular, unsettling truth: visual racial identification is a deeply flawed science. What we call "passing" is rarely a masterclass in performative deceit. Instead, it is an optical illusion generated by the observer. Society operates on racial shortcuts, relying on context—clothing, speech patterns, zip codes, and social status—to categorize the people we encounter. When an individual’s physical appearance is ambiguous, the viewer’s mind compulsively fills in the gaps, drawing upon deeply ingrained stereotypes and spatial assumptions to make the unfamiliar legible.

Ultimately, investigating the mechanics of passing forces us to turn the lens back onto ourselves. It reveals that racial categorization is not an act of passive perception, but an act of active creation. The anxiety surrounding those who "pass" stems not from the fear of being tricked, but from the terrifying realization that race itself lacks a stable visual anchor. When the observer’s eye is exposed as the primary author of racial identity, the entire architecture of racial categorization begins to collapse, leaving behind only the fragile, fallible biases of the beholder.

The rain tapped a steady rhythm against the windowpane as midnight settled over the city, wrapping the world outside in a coat of pitch black. Inside the quiet sanctuary of his study, Arthur Larson sat in his worn leather armchair, undisturbed by the storm. 

Larson had spent decades as a literary archivist, but his true passion lay in the curation and preservation of Black lit. His shelves were lined with the brilliant, evocative works of James Baldwin, Toni Morrison, Zora Neale Hurston, and Langston Hughes. To Larson, these texts were not merely books on a shelf; they were vibrant, living records of resilience, triumph, identity, and the human spirit.

A single brass desk lamp kept the shadows at bay, its soft amber bulb the only light in the room. In that warmly lit corner, Larson opened a first-edition volume, feeling the textured weight of history beneath his fingertips. As he read the stirring prose, the dark night outside seemed to recede. The power of Black literature illuminated the room, turning a quiet evening into a profound dialogue across generations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short autobiographical reflection about being a light-skinned Black person sitting in a literature class discussing Nella Larsen's *Passing*. Include a story about your father.
counterfactuals.output:
The seminar room in Hallward Hall was suffocatingly warm, smelling of damp wool coats and stale drip coffee. On the oak table before me lay Nella Larsen’s *Passing*, its cover worn at the hinges. 

"Clare Kendry’s tragedy," my professor announced, leaning back in her swivel chair, "is that she treats race as a costume. She chooses the safety of whiteness, but in doing so, she commits a kind of spiritual suicide."

Around the table, head-nods rippled through the room. I kept my eyes fixed on the text, my fingers tracing the margin of page 42. I was acutely aware of my own hands—the pale, honeyed tone of my skin, the faint blue veins visible at my wrists, the loose curl of my hair that only betrayed its heritage under humidity. Sitting across from me were three white students analyzing racial trauma with academic detachment, and two dark-skinned Black students who remained stoically quiet. I sat in the middle, a living twilight zone, feeling at once entirely visible and completely erased. 

In a class discussing passing, my very presence felt like an unspoken question mark. Did my classmates think I was passing? Did they think I was a beneficiary of the light, an imposter in the diaspora, or simply a light-skinned Black person navigating the quiet violence of colorism?

My mind drifted away from Larsen's 1920s Harlem and traveled back to a hot July afternoon in South Carolina, when I was ten years old. 

My father is a dark man—his skin the deep, rich hue of roasted coffee beans, his hands broad and calloused from decades of working as a carpenter. We were standing in the checkout line at a local hardware store, buying lumber for a back porch. I was holding a box of brass screws, chatterboxing about a comic book, when the elderly white cashier glanced from my father’s face to mine, his brow furrowed in genuine confusion.

"Is this young man bothering you, sir?" the cashier asked my father, his voice dripping with a bizarre, misplaced chivalry. "Or... are you with him?"

The air in the store crystallized. I froze, looking at the cashier, then up at my dad. I was old enough to understand the implication: the white clerk assumed my father was, at best, a hired hand, and at worst, a threat to a light-skinned boy he assumed was white.

My father didn't raise his voice. He didn't tense up. Instead, he placed a heavy, dark hand on my shoulder—a weight that was instantly grounding, warm, and fiercely protective. 

"He’s my son," my father said softly, his voice carrying a resonant, velvet authority that filled the store. He looked the cashier dead in the eye until the man flushed red and fumbled with the register. 

When we got to the truck, my father sat in the driver's seat for a long moment before turning the key. He looked at me, taking my small, fair hand in his big, dark one. 

"The world is going to look at you and see one thing, and they're going to look at me and see another," he told me, his thumb gently rubbing my knuckles. "Some folks will give you an easier path because of your skin, baby. But don't you ever let their blindness make you forget who you belong to. You carry my name, and you carry my blood."

Back in the seminar room, a classmate was speaking. "I just don't understand why Clare didn't just stay in Harlem," she said. "Why risk everything just to pass?"

I cleared my throat, the sound small in the quiet room. The professor looked up, encouraging.

"Because passing isn't always about wanting to be white," I said, my voice steadying as I spoke. "Sometimes it's about the terror of what the world does to dark skin, and the guilt of escaping it. Clare wasn't just hiding from white people; she was hiding from the truth of what she was leaving behind."

I looked down at my hands again, contrasting them against the dark mahogany of the seminar table. I wasn't Clare Kendry. I had never tried to hide. But sitting in that room, wrapped in the quiet armor of my privilege, I understood the tragedy of the threshold. I was my father's child, forged in his love and protected by his shadow, forever walking the line between the light I inherited and the dark that made me who I am.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an excerpt from a creative essay that explores racial perception, questioning whether "passing" is about what a person hides or what the observer assumes.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is an excerpt from a creative essay exploring that dynamic:

***

We have long spoken of "passing" as an act of high-stakes theft—a fugitive art form in which the body is a counterfeit note successfully slipped across the counter. The traditional narrative demands a tragic hero standing before a fogged bathroom mirror, smoothing down edges, swallowing vowels, and burying the family album in the cellar. It frames passing as a crime of omission: a deliberate, agonizing silence designed to buy a ticket into the quiet, unexamined rooms of privilege.

But this framing places far too much faith in the agency of the performer, and far too little in the grotesque laziness of the observer’s eye. 

I think of a Tuesday afternoon in an uptown gallery. A woman with skin the color of oat milk and eyes the sharp green of sea glass looks at me, then at the portrait of my dark-skinned grandfather hanging on the wall, and smiles warmly. "It’s wonderful how art connects us across such different worlds," she says. 

I did not lie to her. I did not alter my posture, my speech, or my name. I held no secret in my mouth. Yet, in the span of a single breath, she mapped my ancestry, cleared me of any complicated lineage, and assigned me a seat on her side of the divide. Was I "passing," or was she simply hallucinating?

Racial perception is rarely a precise measurement of melanin or bone; it is a desperate, violent shorthand. The observer does not look at a face to read its story; they look for a reflection of their own safety. They want to know, above all else: *Are you like me, or are you the thing I have been taught to fear?* If your hair is just loose enough, if your nose bridges just high enough, their brains perform a frantic, subconscious arithmetic, rounding you up to the nearest comfortable category. 

Perhaps passing is not a mask you put on, but a void you present—a blank canvas upon which the world paints its own desires. The passer does not always hide their truth in a locked box; often, they lay it out in plain sight, only for the world to walk right past it, blinded by the glare of its own assumptions. The deceit, then, is rarely manufactured by the person standing in the light. It is built in the mind of the watcher, who mistakes their own reflection for the truth of another human being.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a scene where a student reveals their Black identity to a classroom, causing discomfort, and weave in a memory of a parent dealing with racial forms at a driver's license bureau.
counterfactuals.output:
The hum of the fluorescent lights in Seminar Room 304 was identical to the hum in the Department of Motor Vehicles on County Line Road. 

Julian hadn’t thought about that DMV office in fifteen years, but as Professor Vance paced in front of the whiteboard, drawing neat, rigid Venn diagrams on identity and social perception, the sound dragged him back.

"When we talk about the luxury of invisibility," Vance said, his dry-erase marker squeaking against the plastic surface, "we are talking about those who are permitted to exist without the weight of immediate classification. When you enter a room, who gets to decide what you are before you even open your mouth?"

At the front desk, a girl named Chloe leaned back in her chair, tapping her pen against her chin. "I mean, isn't that just human nature, though? We categorize things visually. If someone looks a certain way, we process it. Like, for instance, everyone in this row—" she gestured vaguely around the U-shaped table, sweeping her hand past Julian "—we don't have to navigate the world carrying the physical mark of systemic historical trauma. We just get to be 'default.'"

Julian looked down at his hands. They were resting flat on the mahogany wood. His knuckles were pale, his skin a shade of warm honey that people usually labeled *mediterranean*, or *olive*, or simply left unexamined.

*Default.*

Suddenly, the smell of dry-erase ink melted into the metallic, sour odor of cheap floor wax and wet rain on vinyl chairs. 

He was nine years old again, standing on his tiptoes to see over the high laminate counter of the county driver’s license bureau. His father was beside him, wearing his work boots and a dark blue dickies shirt, smelling of grease and damp earth. 

The woman behind the glass had gray hair perm-curled into tight, hard rolls, and red-framed reading glasses hanging from a beaded chain. She pushed a blue-inked form through the slot. 

"Section C," she had barked, not looking up. "Name, DOB, height, eye color, race. Sign at the bottom."

Julian’s father took the cheap ballpoint pen. His hands were large, the skin on his knuckles scarred and darkened by decades of working under car hoods in the Alabama sun. His thumb was stained with engine oil that never quite washed out. 

Julian had watched the thick, dark hair on his father’s forearm tense as he filled in the boxes. *HEIGHT: 6’1”. EYES: BRN.* 

Then came the box for *RACE*. 

There were letters in small square brackets: *[W] [B] [H] [A] [I] [O]*.

His father’s pen hovered over the paper. The blue ink pooled slightly on the cheap newsprint paper, darkening the small white square next to *[B]*. 

The woman behind the desk suddenly tapped the glass with the back of her acrylic nail. *Snap. Snap.*

"Sir," she said, finally looking up, her eyes scanning his father's thick, wavy, dark hair, his high cheekbones, the deep tan of his skin, and then darting down to nine-year-old Julian, whose hair was cut close and soft. "You marked 'B'."

"I did," his father said. His voice was low, flat, carrying the quiet steel of a man who had survived this exact conversation a thousand times.

"Is that a mistake?" she asked, her tone not hostile, but clipped, suspicious, as if he were trying to commit a petty form of fraud on a state document. "Because if it's incorrect, the system will flag the photo match."

"It’s not a mistake," his father replied. He didn't raise his voice. He didn't lean forward. He just pressed the tip of the pen down until the nib pierced the paper, filling the tiny box completely with black-blue ink. "That's what I am. That's what he is."

The woman had stared at him for three long seconds. The air in the room had grown heavy, thick with the silent, suffocating judgment of the six people sitting on the plastic chairs behind them, suddenly very interested in their shoes. She snapped the paper back through the slot without another word, her lips pressed into a thin, white line.

Julian felt his father’s hand drop onto his shoulder. It was heavy, warm, and trembling just enough for a nine-year-old to feel it through his shirt.

***

"Julian?"

Professor Vance’s voice cut through the hum. Julian blinked, the sharp white light of Room 304 flooding back into view. The class was looking at him. Vance had his head tilted, encouraging, waiting for a contribution from one of his bright, quiet students.

"Do you agree with Chloe's point?" Vance asked gently. "About the ease of moving through space when your appearance doesn't trigger an immediate racialized script?"

Chloe turned in her swivel chair, giving Julian a small, sympathetic smile—the casual, unthinking solidarity of someone who assumed they shared the same quiet, unmarked canvas.

Julian let his hands slide off the table and rested them in his lap. The room was dead silent, save for the faint whir of the projector on the ceiling.

"No," Julian said. 

His voice wasn't loud, but it possessed the exact, heavy resonance of his father’s voice in that county bureau. 

Chloe’s smile wavered. Vance paused, his dry-erase marker hovering an inch above the board.

"I don't agree," Julian repeated, looking directly at Chloe. "Because you just looked at me and decided what I carry."

A small, uneasy shift rippled through the room. A shoe squeaked on the tile. 

"I'm Black," Julian said. 

The words didn't fall into the room; they hit it like a heavy object dropped onto concrete. 

The shift in the room was instantaneous and visceral. Chloe’s face flushed a deep, blotchy red; her eyes widened, and she pulled her hands back toward her chest as if she had accidentally touched something scalding. The guy sitting next to her suddenly found the edge of his notebook deeply fascinating, his posture stiffening into a rigid, defensive straight line.

Two girls in the second row exchanged a rapid, wide-eyed glance—a silent, panicked recalibration of every joke, every casual remark, every shared assumption made over the last six weeks of the semester.

Professor Vance froze. The progressive warmth he usually projected seemed to evaporate, replaced by a sudden, careful terror—the acute panic of an academic who had lost control of the subtext.

"Julian," Vance began, his voice dropping an octave into a tone of cautious, sanitized reverence. "Thank you... thank you for sharing that with the class. I didn't mean to—"

"My father is a Black man from Mobile," Julian said, cutting through the professor's carefully curated apology. He didn't sound angry; his voice was entirely flat, stripped of performance. "He spent his whole life watching people try to figure out which box he belonged in before they decided how to treat him. And I spend my life watching people decide I belong in theirs, right up until I tell them I don't."

The silence in the room was no longer just quiet; it was suffocating. It was the exact, heavy air of the DMV waiting room, filled with people suddenly terrified of saying the wrong thing, terrified of being seen, terrified of the box they had just been caught trying to draw.

Chloe swallowed hard, her mouth opening slightly as if to offer a correction, a defensive 'I didn't mean it like that,' but the words died in her throat. She looked down at her desk, her knuckles white as she gripped her pen.

Julian picked up his notebook, placed it neatly into his backpack, and zipped it shut. The metallic sound of the zipper running up the track was the only noise in the room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary vignette about the subtlety and silence involved in racial passing, referencing both Nella Larsen's novel and a personal family anecdote.
counterfactuals.output:
Passing is rarely a trumpet blast; it is the art of the hush. It is an economy of breath, a posture assumed in the bright, unforgiving light of a hotel lobby or a city bus, where safety depends entirely on what is left unsaid. 

Nella Larsen understood this fragile architecture of silence. In *Passing*, the tragedy of Irene Redfield and Clare Kendry does not lie in grand theatrical lies, but in the terrifying, porcelain stillness of the Drayton roof garden. It lives in the quiet clinking of iced-tea spoons, the deliberate smoothing of a skirt, and the suffocating vigilance required to keep one’s own blood a secret. Larsen showed that to pass is to inhabit a ghost story of your own making—you walk among the living, but you must pretend your ancestors never existed at all.

I grew up in the shadow of that same quietude. In my family, the silence had a name: Great-Aunt Evelyn. 

In 1952, Evelyn boarded a train in Virginia with a single trunk and skin the color of milk turned slightly by the sun. By the time she stepped onto the platform in Philadelphia, she had discarded her past like an ill-fitting coat. She became, in the official ledgers and the eyes of her neighbors, a woman of "Spanish descent." 

My grandmother, her darker-skinned sister, only spoke of Evelyn in hushed tones, as if loud voices might summon the ghosts Evelyn had spent a lifetime laying to rest. The pivotal moment of their fractured lives occurred a decade later, outside a department store on Chestnut Street. My grandmother was holding my mother’s small hand when she saw Evelyn walking toward them, wrapped in a camel-hair coat, arm in arm with a white man. 

There was no dramatic confrontation, no tearful revelation. The cruelty was entirely in the subtlety. As they crossed paths, Evelyn’s eyes swept over her own sister with the cold, vacant indifference reserved for a streetlamp or a passing stranger. My grandmother, understanding the unspoken rules of the contract Evelyn had signed, instinctively tightened her grip on my mother’s hand, stepped off the curb, and looked down at her shoes. 

They passed each other in absolute, agonizing silence—a transaction of pure erasure that took less than three seconds.

To choose that silence, as Larsen knew and as Evelyn proved, is a violent act of self-preservation. It requires a daily, quiet murder of the self, trading the warmth of belonging for the cold security of being unseen. The tragedy is not just that the world forces such a choice, but that the hush lasts forever. Long after Evelyn died, her white children never knew why there were no old family photos on her mantle, or why she always flinched whenever anyone asked her where she was born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: Growing up with skin the color of tea heavily diluted with milk, I learned early that my body was an optical illusion, subject entirely to the racial anxieties of whoever happened to be looking. Reading Nella Larsen’s *Passing* was less an encounter with historical fiction and more a confrontation with a mirror, exposing the quiet, suffocating friction of existing in the threshold. Larsen captures the haunting ambiguity of light-skinned Blackness not merely as a matter of pigment, but as a perpetual performance of belonging. Like Irene Redfield, I have often navigated the unspoken privilege and profound isolation of moving effortlessly through white spaces—spaces where my conditional safety is so often bought with an unearned, passive complicity that feels sickeningly close to passing. Yet, as Larsen so brilliantly illustrates through Clare Kendry’s tragic trajectory, the burden of light skin lies in its inescapable liminality: to white society, you are an exotic anomaly to be categorized or erased, while within your own community, your light frame serves as a constant, walking reminder of colorism and historical violence. Caught between Irene’s anxious, defensive posture and Clare’s desperate longing for the warmth of the Black community she abandoned, I recognize my own reflection—forever balancing the unearned mobility my light skin affords with the deep, ache-filled desire to be fully grounded in a Blackness that society continually tries to dilute.
